title: uuid with uuidv7() (PG 18); identity columns vs serial
summary: Use bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY for internal keys and uuid DEFAULT uuidv7() when ids are minted outside one database or shown to users; serial is the legacy shorthand. Version 7 UUIDs sort by creation time, random version 4 UUIDs don't.

examples.title: Identity columns: gaps, the backing sequence, and GENERATED ALWAYS

annotations.note: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY is the SQL-standard auto-increment. It implies NOT NULL but not uniqueness (the docs are explicit about that), which is what PRIMARY KEY adds. bigint, for the reasons in the previous lesson.

The rolled-back insert consumed id 3, so the next row gets 4. A sequence never takes a value back, because that would make every inserting transaction wait for the others. Gaps also come from crashes and from INSERT ... ON CONFLICT: sequence values are unique, not gapless.

An identity column still draws from a sequence (tickets_id_seq). The difference to serial is ownership: the column manages it, and you restart it with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN id RESTART instead of finding and altering a separate object.
SQLSTATE 428C9. With ALWAYS, an explicit id needs INSERT ... OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE, so a hand-written id is always a visible decision. GENERATED BY DEFAULT would accept it silently, like serial.

examples.title: serial: a column default, and how imports break it

annotations.note: The docs say the serial types "are not true types, but merely a notational convenience": an integer column (so 2,147,483,647 is the ceiling), a sequence object, and a DEFAULT nextval(...). bigserial gives bigint.
The catalog sees an integer column with a default; is_identity is NO. Copying the table definition elsewhere, or granting other roles access, means dealing with that separate sequence too.
Explicit ids are just values overriding a default, so nothing objects. This is how migrations from other systems and test fixtures insert their rows.

SQLSTATE 23505: nextval() returns 1, which the import already used. The fix after any manual load is setval(pg_get_serial_sequence(...), max(id)); with an identity column the same holds after an OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE load, but at least the load had to say so.

examples.title: uuidv7() vs uuidv4(): sort order, embedded time, size

annotations.note: uuidv7() is new in PostgreSQL 18. No sequence and no coordination: any session, service or client can mint ids, and RFC 9562 defines the format, so ids made elsewhere are interchangeable with these.

A v7 UUID starts with a millisecond Unix timestamp, then (in PostgreSQL's generator) a sub-millisecond fraction, then random bits, and the generator never steps back within a session, so 1000 ids from one statement sort in creation order. v4 is 122 random bits: new keys land on random pages of the primary-key index instead of at its right edge, which costs cache and write volume on big tables.

Versions 7 and 4, read from the id itself. uuid_extract_timestamp() recovers a v7 id's creation time (to the millisecond) and returns NULL for v4. Handy for debugging; a leak if the id appears in a public URL and creation times are sensitive.

A uuid is 16 bytes, twice a bigint; as text it would be 36 characters plus overhead, compared case-sensitively. The optional shift argument moves the embedded time, so backfilled historic rows can get ids that sort where they belong.

use_cases: bigint identity: internal primary keys, join-heavy tables, ids people read aloud in support tickets
uuidv7: ids minted by clients or several services before the insert, rows merged from several databases, offline-first apps
uuidv4: public tokens and ids where neither order nor creation time may leak
strengths: Identity columns are standard SQL and, with GENERATED ALWAYS, refuse accidental hand-written ids; serial is a Postgres-only macro that refuses nothing
uuidv7 needs no central counter, yet keys still sort by creation time and append to the index like a sequence
uuid is a native 16-byte type with its own comparison and index support, not a 36-character string
Generating ids in the database (DEFAULT plus RETURNING) means the application needs no id library and no extra round trip
weaknesses: A uuid is twice the size of a bigint, in the table and again in every index and foreign key that refers to it
A v7 id reveals when its row was created
Sequences have gaps (rollbacks, ON CONFLICT, crashes), so no generated key is a gapless counter
UUIDs are hard to read in logs and impossible to dictate over the phone; ticket 4211 is not

pitfalls.title: serial (or BY DEFAULT identity) plus hand-written ids
pitfalls.detail: Imports and fixtures insert explicit ids, the sequence doesn't move, and the first ordinary insert collides. Resynchronize after every manual load.

pitfalls.title: Using a sequence for invoice numbers
pitfalls.detail: The docs state that sequences cannot produce gapless numbering. If the law requires consecutive numbers, keep a counter row and update it in the same transaction as the invoice, accepting that those transactions serialize.

pitfalls.title: UUIDs stored as text
pitfalls.detail: More than twice the size, slower comparisons, and 'A0EE...' vs 'a0ee...' compare unequal as text. The uuid type accepts both spellings and stores one value.
pitfalls.bad: id text PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()::text
pitfalls.good: id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7()

pitfalls.title: Reading id order as commit order
pitfalls.detail: With any generated key, a transaction that took its id first can commit last. A consumer that remembers 'the highest id I have seen' can miss rows committed later with smaller ids.

quiz.q: An insert into a table with an identity id is rolled back. What happens to the id value it used?
options: It's lost; the next insert gets the following value
The rollback fails until the sequence is reset
quiz.why: nextval() results are not reclaimed when a transaction aborts, so sequences have gaps.

quiz.q: id is GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY. Which insert of id 10 succeeds?
options: INSERT INTO t (id, title) OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE VALUES (10, 'x')
Neither: ALWAYS never accepts explicit values
quiz.why: ALWAYS accepts a user-specified value only when the INSERT says OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE.

quiz.q: Why are uuidv7 primary keys kinder to a B-tree index than uuidv4?
options: They start with a timestamp, so new keys arrive in order at the end of the index
quiz.why: Both are 16 bytes and practically unique; v7's time prefix makes inserts append like a sequence instead of scattering.
gen_random_uuid() makes a version 4 UUID, which has no timestamp; the function returns NULL for versions other than 1 and 7.

body:
## Concept

Surrogate keys come in two families:

- **Counters**, drawn from a sequence. `bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` is the
  standard way since PostgreSQL 10; `serial`/`bigserial` is the older shorthand that
  expands to a column default calling `nextval()`. Both use a sequence object, and
  sequences hand out each value once, gaps included, without waiting for other
  transactions.
- **UUIDs**, 128-bit values anyone can generate without asking anyone. PostgreSQL 18 adds
  `uuidv7()`, a time-ordered UUID (millisecond timestamp first), next to `uuidv4()` (an
  alias of `gen_random_uuid()`). Ordered ids keep the primary-key index appending at one
  end, the way a sequence does, without the sequence.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java, Python, JS:** the built-in generators you know (`UUID.randomUUID()`,
  `uuid.uuid4()`, `crypto.randomUUID()`) make version 4: random, unordered. Fine for
  tokens, poor as a clustered sort order.
- **ORMs:** "auto-increment" maps to an identity column. If an ORM or an old tutorial
  generates `serial`, it works, but it's the legacy form.
- **Go:** `DEFAULT uuidv7()` plus `INSERT ... RETURNING id` lets the database mint the id,
  so the service needs no UUID library just for keys.
- **C:** think of a uuid as a 16-byte array compared like `memcmp`; v7 puts a big-endian
  timestamp in the first 6 bytes, which is why byte order equals time order.

## Design notes

A sensible default: `bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` for internal keys. Reach for
`uuid DEFAULT uuidv7()` when ids are created outside a single database (clients that work
offline, several services, merging data) or when sequential ids would leak volume ("order
4211" says you have had about 4,200 orders). Choose ALWAYS over BY DEFAULT unless loading
ids from elsewhere is routine; making the override explicit is the point.

v7 order is time order at millisecond granularity, which is what the docs promise.
PostgreSQL 18's generator additionally fills the next 12 bits with a sub-millisecond
fraction and keeps each new value above the previous one generated in the same session,
which is why the example's 1000 ids sort perfectly. The docs only list the parts
("millisecond precision + sub-millisecond timestamp + random"); the per-session step is
in the source (src/backend/utils/adt/uuid.c, function get_real_time_ns_ascending), and
on PostgreSQL 18.7 here 100,000 ids from one statement, about 960 per millisecond, came
out strictly increasing. Across sessions there is no such promise: ids are ordered by
the clock reading they embed, millisecond then fraction, and random bits only decide
between ids generated within about a microsecond of each other. That is roughly the order in which they were
generated, not the order in which their transactions commit.

The embedded timestamp is the price of that order. If creation time is sensitive, keep v7
as the internal key and expose a separate random token, or use v4 and accept the index
cost.

files.examples/03_uuidv7.sql:
CREATE TABLE events (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(),  -- time-ordered (PostgreSQL 18)
  n  int  NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE events_v4 (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv4(),  -- random; same as gen_random_uuid()
  n  int  NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO events    (n) SELECT g FROM generate_series(1, 1000) AS g;
INSERT INTO events_v4 (n) SELECT g FROM generate_series(1, 1000) AS g;

-- Generated ids differ on every run, so look at their properties.
-- Does ORDER BY id give back the insertion order?
SELECT 'uuidv7' AS generator,
       array_agg(n ORDER BY id) = array_agg(n ORDER BY n) AS id_order_is_insert_order
FROM events
UNION ALL
SELECT 'uuidv4', array_agg(n ORDER BY id) = array_agg(n ORDER BY n)
FROM events_v4
ORDER BY generator;

-- A v7 id carries its creation time; a v4 id carries nothing but randomness.
SELECT uuid_extract_version(v7) AS v7_version,
       uuid_extract_timestamp(v7) BETWEEN now() - interval '1 minute'
                                      AND now() + interval '1 minute' AS v7_time_is_now,
       uuid_extract_version(v4) AS v4_version,
       uuid_extract_timestamp(v4) AS v4_time
FROM (SELECT uuidv7() AS v7, uuidv4() AS v4) AS ids;

-- 16 bytes as uuid, 36 characters as text. And shift backdates the
-- embedded time, e.g. when backfilling ids for historic rows.
SELECT pg_column_size(uuidv7()) AS uuid_bytes,
       length(uuidv7()::text) AS text_chars,
       uuidv7(interval '-1 day') < (SELECT id FROM events ORDER BY id LIMIT 1) AS backdated_sorts_first;
